title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
content: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus establishes that differentiation and integration are inverse operations. Part 1 states that if f is continuous on [a, b], then the function g(x) = ∫[a to x] f(t)dt is differentiable and g'(x) = f(x). Part 2 states that ∫[a to b] f(x)dx = F(b) - F(a), where F is any antiderivative of f such that F'(x) = f(x). This theorem provides the algebraic foundation for calculating definite integrals.

title: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
content: In linear algebra, the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of any real m x n matrix A is a factorization of the form A = U Σ V^T, where U is an m x m orthogonal matrix containing left-singular vectors, Σ is an m x n rectangular diagonal matrix containing non-negative singular values ordered in descending magnitude, and V is an n x n orthogonal matrix containing right-singular vectors. SVD is fundamental to principal component analysis (PCA), pseudoinverses, data compression, and modern machine learning embeddings.

title: Maxwell's Equations of Classical Electromagnetism
content: Maxwell's Equations are four fundamental differential equations that describe how electric and magnetic fields are generated by charges and currents, and how they interact: 1) Gauss's Law (∇·E = ρ/ε₀): electric flux depends on enclosed charge; 2) Gauss's Law for Magnetism (∇·B = 0): there are no magnetic monopoles; 3) Maxwell-Faraday Induction (∇×E = -∂B/∂t): changing magnetic fields induce electric fields; 4) Ampère's Circuital Law with Maxwell's addition (∇×B = μ₀J + μ₀ε₀∂E/∂t): currents and displacement currents produce magnetic fields. They predict electromagnetic waves propagating at the speed of light c.

title: The Laws of Thermodynamics
content: Thermodynamics governs heat, work, temperature, and energy transfer: 0) Zeroth Law: If two systems are in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other (defines temperature); 1) First Law: Energy cannot be created or destroyed (ΔU = Q - W); 2) Second Law: The total entropy of an isolated system always increases over time (ΔS_universe ≥ 0); 3) Third Law: As temperature approaches absolute zero (0 Kelvin), the entropy of a pure crystalline substance approaches a constant minimum (zero).

title: Schrödinger Equation and Wavefunction Collapse
content: The time-dependent Schrödinger equation (iℏ ∂Ψ/∂t = ĤΨ) is the fundamental governing equation of non-relativistic quantum mechanics, where Ψ is the quantum state wavefunction and Ĥ is the Hamiltonian operator representing total system energy. The Born rule states that the probability density of finding a particle at position r is given by |Ψ(r, t)|². Superposition allows states to exist in linear combinations until measurement, which triggers wavefunction collapse or decoherence into classical observables.

title: Semiconductor Physics, Band Gaps, and P-N Junctions
content: Semiconductors have electrical conductivity between conductors and insulators, determined by their electronic band gap (E_g)—the energy difference between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band. At absolute zero, the conduction band is empty; thermal or optical excitation promotes electrons across the band gap, creating mobile electron-hole pairs. Doping introduces donors (n-type) or acceptors (p-type). A p-n junction creates a depletion region with a built-in electric field, enabling diodes, bipolar transistors, MOSFETs, solar cells, and LEDs.

title: DNA Structure and the Central Dogma of Molecular Biology
content: Described by Watson, Crick, and Franklin in 1953, DNA consists of two complementary antiparallel polynucleotide strands coiled around a common axis in a right-handed double helix, stabilized by hydrogen bonding between nitrogenous base pairs: Adenine pairs with Thymine (A-T), and Guanine pairs with Cytosine (G-C). The Central Dogma (formulated by Francis Crick) states that genetic information flows directionally from DNA to RNA via transcription, and from messenger RNA (mRNA) to polypeptide proteins via ribosomal translation.
